question: The Spanish Civil Guard’s Central Operational Unit (UCO) has obtained a file from public company ADIF on a contract awarded to Levantina Ingeniería y Construcción SL (B97016125) as part of corruption investigations into the Sánchez Government (Koldo case). The file contains suspected payments linked to contracts awarded by the Directorate-General for Roads1.

Between 2021 and 2023, the company was awarded at least three contracts by the government worth EUR 4.4 million for works funded by the ERDF or under NextGenerationEU2. Given that former senior government officials are in prison for bribery, embezzlement and influence peddling in relation to public contracts: 1.
Will the Commission investigate whether alleged corrupt practices linked to former senior officials in the Sánchez government also involved EU-funded contracts, such as the Levantina contracts?
Will it require Spain to repay the EU funds disbursed for each contract, including the company’s share in joint ventures if wrongdoing is detected?
Following all the cases of corruption surrounding Pedro Sánchez, has the Commission launched specific audits to ensure that EU funds allocated by the Spanish Government have not been misappropriated?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026) The Commission has zero tolerance for fraud affecting the EU budget, including funds such as NextGenerationEU and the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), and expects the same level of commitment from Member States. The protection of the EU’s budget is a shared responsibility.

Member States are primarily responsible for ensuring that expenditure financed from both the NextGenerationEU and Cohesion policy funds complies with applicable EU and national rules, including rules on public procurement, conflicts of interest, fraud and corruption, and for preventing, detecting, correcting and reporting on irregularities, including fraud.

The Commission exercises its supervisory role by assessing the effectiveness of national management and control systems and through its own audits to confirm that Member States are fulfilling their obligations and that funds are being appropriately implemented.

If the Commission were to receive sufficiently substantiated information indicating a breach of applicable rules or a risk to the financial interest of the EU, it would assess the matter and, where appropriate, make use of the instruments available under the relevant legal framework.

Allegations of criminal conduct fall within the competence of the relevant national authorities and, where applicable, of the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) and/or the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), acting within their respective mandates1.
1Article 22(5) of the RRF Regulation – PFIU: the Financing and Loan Agreements shall also: provide for the

right of the Commission to reduce proportionately the support under the Facility and recover any amount due to the Union budget or to ask for early repayment of the loan, in cases of fraud, corruption, and conflicts of interests affecting the financial interests of the Union that have not been corrected by the Member State, or a serious breach of an obligation resulting from such agreements.
